1:1.headline: He called: a word of love, written with a small א
1:1.body: Rashi says God called Moses before every message, a loving word the angels use, while to Balaam the Torah writes ויקר, a word of chance meeting. Baal HaTurim says Moses wanted to write ויקר about himself too, so God told him to add the א, and he wrote it small.

sources.quote: לְכָל דִּבְּרוֹת וּלְכָל אֲמִירוֹת וּלְכָל צִוּוּיִים קָדְמָה קְרִיאָה, לְשׁוֹן חִבָּה
sources.says: Rashi says every message to Moses was preceded by a call, a word of affection.

sources.quote: אֲבָל לִנְבִיאֵי אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם נִגְלָה עֲלֵיהֶן בִּלְשׁוֹן עֲרָאִי וְטֻמְאָה, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וַיִּקָּר אֱלֹהִים אֶל בִּלְעָם
sources.says: Rashi says to the prophets of other nations God appeared with a word of chance and impurity, as in God happened upon Balaam.

sources.quote: שמשה לא רצה לכתוב אלא ויקר כדרך שנא' בבלעם כאלו לא נראה לו השם אלא במקרה ואמר לו הקב"ה לכתוב גם באל"ף וכתבה קטנה
sources.says: Baal HaTurim says Moses wanted to write only ויקר, as with Balaam, as if God appeared to him by chance, but God told him to write the א too, and he wrote it small.

sources.quote: ולמה אל"ף זעירא דאזער גרמיה
sources.says: Siftei Kohen says the א is small because Moses made himself small.

1:2.headline: Why say אדם? Like Adam, offer nothing stolen
1:2.body: Rashi asks why the verse says אדם, a person, and hears Adam in it. The first man owned everything, so nothing he offered could be stolen, and neither may your offerings be.

sources.quote: מָה אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן לֹא הִקְרִיב מִן הַגָּזֵל — שֶׁהַכֹּל הָיָה שֶׁלּוֹ — אַף אַתֶּם לֹא תַּקְרִיבוּ מִן הַגָּזֵל
sources.says: Rashi says just as the first man did not offer anything stolen, since everything was his, so you must not offer anything stolen.

1:3.headline: לרצנו: so he is accepted, or of his own free will
1:3.body: Rashbam reads לרצנו as so that he will be accepted, if the animal is whole and brought to the right place. Ibn Ezra reads it as willingly, not by force, and Rashi says they may press him until he says I want to.

sources.quote: לרצונו - אם זכר תמים יקריבנו ולפתח אוהל מועד אז יהיה לו לרצון
sources.says: Rashbam says if he offers an unblemished male at the entrance of the Tent, then it will be accepted for him.

sources.quote: לרצונו לפני ה׳‎. שיקריבנו ברצונו ולא באונס
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means he offers it willingly and not under force.

sources.quote: כּוֹפִין אוֹתוֹ עַד שֶׁיֹּאמַר רוֹצֶה אֲנִי
sources.says: Rashi says they press him until he says I want to.

1:7.headline: Fire came from heaven, yet the priests must bring their own
1:7.body: Rashi says that even though fire came down from heaven onto the altar, there is a commandment for the priests to bring ordinary fire too.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָאֵשׁ יוֹרֶדֶת מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם מִצְוָה לְהָבִיא מִן הַהֶדְיוֹט
sources.says: Rashi says although fire comes down from heaven, it is a commandment to bring ordinary fire.

1:8.headline: פדר, the fat, read with letters swapped as the divider
1:8.body: Onkelos translates פדר as fat, and Rashi says it was laid over the cut neck as a mark of respect. Ramban says the word has no partner and reads it as פרד with the letters swapped: the thin fat that separates the upper and lower intestines.

sources.quote: יָת רֵישָׁא וְיָת תַּרְבָּא
sources.says: Onkelos translates: the head and the fat.

sources.quote: וּמְכַסֶּה בּוֹ אֶת בֵּית הַשְּׁחִיטָה, וְזֶהוּ דֶּרֶךְ כָּבוֹד שֶׁל מַעְלָה
sources.says: Rashi says the fat covers the place where the animal was cut, which is a way of showing respect to God.

sources.quote: וְאֵין לַמִּלָּה חָבֵר
sources.says: Ramban says the word has no partner elsewhere.

sources.quote: וְהַמִּלָּה מִן הַהֲפוּכִים, פֶּדֶר - פֶּרֶד, שֶׁמַּפְרִיד בֵּין הַקְּרָבַיִם הָעֶלְיוֹנִים לַתַּחְתּוֹנִים
sources.says: Ramban says the word has its letters reversed, פדר for פרד, because it separates the upper intestines from the lower.

1:9.headline: Onkelos uses a different word for washing the innards
1:9.body: When people wash, Onkelos writes יסחי, to bathe. For the animal's innards he writes יחליל, which Chizkuni explains as clearing out the waste so they are left hollow.

sources.quote: וְגַוֵיהּ וּכְרָעוֹהִי יְחַלֵּל בְּמַיָּא
sources.says: Onkelos translates: its innards and its legs he shall rinse out in water.

sources.quote: אבל רחיצה האמורה בקרבנות מתרגמינן ״‎יחליל״‎ פירוש יוציא מהן הפרש וישארו חלולים
sources.says: Chizkuni says washing in offerings is translated יחליל, meaning he removes the waste so they are left hollow.

sources.quote: ירחץ במים. רחיצה האמורה גבי אדם מתרגמינן ״‎יסחי״‎
sources.says: Chizkuni says washing said of a person is translated יסחי.

1:9.headline: A pleasing smell: contentment that God's word was done
1:9.body: Rashi reads ניחוח, pleasing, as נחת רוח, contentment. God is content that He spoke and His will was done.

sources.quote: ניחוח. נַחַת רוּחַ לְפָנַי, שֶׁאָמַרְתִּי וְנַעֲשָֹה רְצוֹנִי
sources.says: Rashi says it means contentment before me, that I spoke and my will was done.

1:15.headline: מלק: a word known only from the sages' tradition
1:15.body: Ibn Ezra says ומלק appears nowhere else in the Bible, so how it was done is known only from tradition. Rashi gives that tradition: no knife, the priest cuts with his own fingernail from the back of the neck.

sources.quote: ומלק. אין לו אח במקרא ומשפט המליקה מדברי הקבלה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word has no partner in Scripture, and how מליקה is done comes from tradition.

sources.quote: אֵין מְלִיקָה בִּכְלִי אֶלָּא בְּעַצְמוֹ שֶׁל כֹּהֵן, קוֹצֵץ בְּצִפָּרְנוֹ מִמּוּל הָעֹרֶף
sources.says: Rashi says it is not done with a tool but by the priest himself, cutting with his fingernail from the back of the neck.

1:15.headline: ונמצה: the blood is squeezed out against the altar wall
1:15.body: Rashi ties ונמצה to מיץ, squeezing: the priest presses the cut against the altar wall and the blood drains down. Tur HaArokh explains why: a bird has so little blood that it would stick to a bowl.

sources.quote: כּוֹבֵשׁ בֵּית הַשְּׁחִיטָה עַל קִיר הַמִּזְבֵּחַ וְהַדָּם מִתְמַצֶּה וְיוֹרֵד
sources.says: Rashi says he presses the cut against the altar wall and the blood is squeezed out and runs down.

sources.quote: ונמצה דמו. לְשׁוֹן מִיץ אַפַּיִם
sources.says: Rashi says ונמצה is the language of squeezing, as in squeezing the nose.

sources.quote: לפי שהדם הוא מעט ואם יקבלנו במזרק ידבק בו
sources.says: Tur HaArokh says the blood is little, and if collected in a bowl it would stick to it.

1:16.headline: בנצתה: with its feathers, or with its filth
1:16.body: Ibn Ezra reads בנצתה as with its feathers, from נוצה. Rashi reads it as with its innards, from a word for something disgusting, and notes that Onkelos translates it as with its food.

sources.quote: בנצתה. עם הנוצה שלו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means with its feathers.

sources.quote: עִם בְּנֵי מֵעֶיהָ, וְנוֹצָה לְשׁוֹן דָּבָר הַמָּאוּס
sources.says: Rashi says it means with its innards, and נוצה is a word for something disgusting.

sources.quote: וְיַעֲדֵּי יָת זְפָקֵיהּ בְּאוּכְלֵיהּ
sources.says: Onkelos translates: he removes its crop with its food.

1:17.headline: Feathers and all: so the poor man's offering looks full
1:17.body: Rashi says the bird is burned with its feathers, though burning feathers smell foul, so that the altar looks full and honored by a poor man's offering. Ramban disagrees: כנפיו means its wings, showing where to split the bird, not its feathers.

sources.quote: וַהֲלֹא אֵין לְךָ הֶדְיוֹט שֶׁמֵּרִיחַ רֵיחַ כְּנָפַיִם נִשְֹרָפִים וְאֵין נַפְשׁוֹ קָצָה עָלָיו
sources.says: Rashi says there is no ordinary person who smells burning feathers and is not disgusted.

sources.quote: כְּדֵי שֶׁיְּהֵא הַמִּזְבֵּחַ שָֹבֵעַ וּמְהֻדָּר בְּקָרְבָּנוֹ שֶׁל עָנִי
sources.says: Rashi says it is so that the altar will be full and adorned with the poor man's offering.

sources.quote: אֲבָל פֵּרוּשׁוֹ וְשִׁסַּע אוֹתוֹ בִּמְקוֹם כְּנָפָיו
sources.says: Ramban says the meaning is that he splits it at the place of its wings.

1:17.headline: A small bird pleases God as much as an ox
1:17.body: Rashi notes that the Torah calls both the bird and the large animal a pleasing smell. Whether one gives much or little, what counts is that the heart is turned to heaven.

sources.quote: לוֹמַר לְךָ אֶחָד הַמַּרְבֶּה וְאֶחָד הַמַּמְעִיט וּבִלְבַד שֶׁיְּכַוֵּן אֶת לִבּוֹ לַשָּׁמַיִם
sources.says: Rashi says it teaches that one who gives much and one who gives little are the same, as long as he directs his heart to heaven.

sources.quote: נאמר ריח ניחוח בעוף הדק כמו בשור הגדול
sources.says: Bekhor Shor says pleasing smell is said of the small bird just as of the big ox.

11:2.headline: 'This is the animal': Moses held each one up and showed it
11:2.body: Rashi stops on זאת, 'this', a word you say while pointing. He says Moses held up each kind of animal, fish, bird and crawling thing and showed Israel: this you may eat, and this you may not.

sources.quote: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁהָיָה מֹשֶׁה אוֹחֵז בַּחַיָּה וּמַרְאֶה אוֹתָהּ לְיִשְֹרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says this teaches that Moses held the animal and showed it to Israel.

11:2.headline: חיה, 'animal', also sounds like 'life'
11:2.body: Rashi hears חיים, 'life', in the word חיה. Israel cling to God and are fit to live, he says, so God set them apart from what is impure.

sources.quote: זאת החיה. לְשׁוֹן חַיִּים, לְפִי שֶׁיִּשְֹרָאֵל דְּבוּקִים בַּמָּקוֹם וּרְאוּיִין לִהְיוֹת חַיִּים
sources.says: Rashi says חיה is the language of life, because Israel cling to God and are worthy of life.

11:7.headline: חזיר, the pig, and a promise that something will 'return'
11:7.body: Rabbeinu Bahya quotes a midrash that hears להחזיר, 'to return', in חזיר. Some versions say God will return the pig to Israel. Bahya warns this does not mean the pig will become kosher: the power it stands for will one day help Israel.

sources.quote: למה נמשלה מלכות זו לחזיר, שעתיד הקב"ה להחזיר עליהן מדת הדין
sources.says: Bahya quotes the Tanchuma: the kingdom is likened to the pig because God will return judgment upon them.

sources.quote: וההמון מבינים שהחזיר יהיה טהור לישראל, אבל באור הענין על הכח שלו
sources.says: Bahya says ordinary people take it to mean the pig will become pure, but it really refers to the power it stands for.

11:13.headline: עזניה: a real bird, not a creature of legend
11:13.body: Ibn Ezra says a Gaon was wrong to translate עזניה as the Anqa, a bird of Arabic legend, since the Torah would not forbid a creature that never existed. Ibn Ezra and Chizkuni read the name from עוז, 'strength'.

sources.quote: טעה הגאון שתרגם אותה אלענקא כי זה השם בלשון ישמעאל על דבר שלא נמצא בעולם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the Gaon erred in translating it as the Anqa, an Arabic name for a thing that does not exist.

sources.quote: ועזניה מן עוז והנו״ן נוסף
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says עזניה comes from עוז, strength, with an added נ.

sources.quote: ועל שם עזותה ועקשותה נקראת כך
sources.says: Chizkuni says it is named for its strength and hardness.

11:17.headline: ינשוף: the owl, named for flying at dusk
11:17.body: Ibn Ezra says the ינשוף flies in the נשף, the dusk, because it cannot see by day in the sun's glare.

sources.quote: ינשוף. עוף יעופף בנשף כי לא יראה ביום מפני להט אור השמש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a bird that flies at dusk, since it cannot see by day because of the sun's glare.

11:18.headline: תנשמת: one name for a bird and for a crawling creature
11:18.body: Rashi says the bird תנשמת looks like a mouse that flies at night, and the crawling תנשמת is like it but has no eyes. Ibn Ezra says the name means that all who see it are appalled, and notes it appears in both lists.

sources.quote: וְתִנְשֶׁמֶת הָאֲמוּרָה בַּשְּׁרָצִים הִיא דוֹמָה לָהּ וְאֵין לָהּ עֵינַיִם
sources.says: Rashi says the תנשמת among the crawling creatures resembles the bird but has no eyes.

sources.quote: התנשמת. כל רואהו ישום גם זה השם נמצא בשרצים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says everyone who sees it is appalled, and that the same name appears among the crawling creatures.

11:19.headline: חסידה, the stork: named for kindness to its friends
11:19.body: Rashi says the stork is called חסידה because it does חסד, kindness, sharing food with its companions. Ibn Ezra reports that some say it spreads kindness over a long way.

sources.quote: וְלָמָּה נִקְרָא שְׁמָהּ חֲסִידָה? שֶׁעוֹשָֹׁה חֲסִידוּת עִם חַבְרוֹתֶיהָ בִּמְזוֹנוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says it is called חסידה because it does kindness with its companions in food.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים שהיא מפזרת חסד בדרך רחוקה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that some say it spreads kindness over a far way.

11:19.headline: דוכיפת: the bird whose crown is folded double
11:19.body: Rashi reads דוכיפת as הודו כפות, 'its glory is folded': its crest is doubled. Rabbeinu Bahya adds the Talmud's story that this bird brought the שמיר, the stone-cutter, for building the Temple.

sources.quote: וְלָמָּה נִקְרָא שְׁמוֹ דּוּכִיפַת? שֶׁ"הוֹדוֹ כָפוּת" וְזוֹ הִיא כַּרְבָּלְתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it is called דוכיפת because its glory, its crest, is folded.

sources.quote: הדוכיפת זה תרנגול הבר שהודו כפול וכרבלתו כפולה, והוא הביא שמיר למקדש
sources.says: Bahya says it is the wild rooster with a doubled crest, and it brought the שמיר to the Temple.

11:22.headline: חרגל: the insect that races with its legs
11:22.body: Chizkuni hears two words inside חרגל: it 'competes' (מתחרה) 'with its legs' (ברגליו) to jump. Ibn Ezra says that if it is one four-letter word, it has no partner in the Bible.

sources.quote: החרגל מתחרה ברגליו לנתר בהם
sources.says: Chizkuni says the חרגל competes with its legs to leap with them.

sources.quote: החרגול. אם היא מרובעת אין לו אח
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says if it is a four-letter word, it has no brother.

11:45.headline: Not 'brought out' but 'brought up': the food laws as a rise
11:45.body: Everywhere else God says He 'brought you out' of Egypt. Rashi notes that here it says 'brought you up', and quotes the sages: freeing Israel just so they would not eat creeping things would have been enough. It is a rise in their standing.

sources.quote: בְּכֻלָּן כְּתִיב "הוֹצֵאתִי" וְכָאן כְּתִיב "הַמַּעֲלֶה"
sources.says: Rashi notes that everywhere it says 'I brought out', but here it says 'who brings up'.

sources.quote: אִלְּמָלֵי לֹא הֶעֱלֵיתִי אֶת יִשְֹרָאֵל מִמִּצְרַיִם אֶלָּא בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁאֵין מִטַּמְּאִין בִּשְׁרָצִים כִּשְׁאָר אֻמּוֹת דַּיָּם
sources.says: Rashi quotes the school of Rabbi Yishmael: had God brought Israel up only so they would not defile themselves with creeping things, it would be enough.

sources.quote: וּמַעַלְיוּתָא הִיא גַּבַּיְהוּ, זֶהוּ לְשׁוֹן מַעֲלָה
sources.says: Rashi says it is an elevation for them, and that is why it uses the word for going up.

13:2.headline: שאת: a burn that rises, or a raised patch of skin
13:2.body: Ibn Ezra reads שאת as a burn, like the word for a fire signal that goes up. Ramban quotes the sages, who read it as a raised patch, and Kli Yakar says this mark comes for pride.

sources.quote: ומלת שאת. כמו שרפה וכן והמשאת החלה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says שאת means a burning, like the fire signal in Judges, perhaps named for fire that rises.

sources.quote: וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ אָמְרוּ (שבועות ו), אֵין שְׂאֵת אֶלָּא לְשׁוֹן גְּבוֹהָה
sources.says: Ramban quotes the sages that שאת only means something high.

sources.quote: אֵין שְׂאֵת אֶלָּא גְּבוֹהָה, וּמִין צָרַעַת זֶה בָּא עַל גַּסּוּת הָרוּחַ
sources.says: Kli Yakar says שאת means high, and this kind of mark comes for arrogance.

13:5.headline: 'Stood in its eyes': the mark's look, or the priest's view?
13:5.body: Rashi reads עין here as the mark's look: it kept its color and size. Ramban cites the sages, who read it as the priest's eyes: as far as he could see, it did not spread.

sources.quote: בְּמַרְאֵהוּ וּבְשִׁעוּרוֹ הָרִאשׁוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says it means the mark kept its first appearance and size.

sources.quote: אִם כֵּן פֵּרוּשׁוֹ וְאִם בְּעֵינֵי הַכֹּהֵן הַנִּזְכָּר עָמַד הַנֶּגַע
sources.says: Ramban, following the sages, reads it as 'in the eyes of the priest' the mark stayed put.

sources.quote: בעיניו של כהן, לפי ראות עיניו עמד ולא פשה
sources.says: Bekhor Shor also reads it as the priest's eyes: by his sight it stayed and did not spread.

13:6.headline: כהה: did the mark fade, or did it hold back?
13:6.body: Rashi says כהה means the mark grew dimmer in color. Ibn Ezra reports that many read it as 'dark', but he takes it as the opposite of spreading.

sources.quote: כהה. הָכְהָה מִמַּרְאִיתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the mark became dimmer than its look before.

sources.quote: ולפי דעתי שמלת כהה הפך פשה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says that in his view כהה is the opposite of 'spread'.

13:14.headline: 'On the day': some days the priest does not look at all
13:14.body: Rashi stops on the extra words 'on the day'. He learns that on some days the priest waits: a groom gets all seven days of his wedding feast, and anyone gets the days of a festival.

sources.quote: לְלַמֵּד יֵשׁ יוֹם שֶׁאַתָּה רוֹאֶה בוֹ וְיֵשׁ יוֹם שֶׁאֵין אַתָּה רוֹאֶה בוֹ, מִכָּאן אָמְרוּ: חָתָן נוֹתְנִין לוֹ כָּל שִׁבְעַת יְמֵי הַמִּשְׁתֶּה
sources.says: Rashi says the word teaches there are days the priest examines and days he does not, so a groom gets his seven feast days.

13:30.headline: צהב: gold, red, or nearly white? Three old readings
13:30.body: Rashi says צהב is like זהב, the color of gold. Onkelos translates it as red, and Ibn Ezra says the Arabic word means close to white.

sources.quote: וּלְשׁוֹן צָהֹב דּוֹמֶה לְתַבְנִית הַזָּהָב
sources.says: Rashi says צהב looks like the form of gold, צהוב like זהוב.

sources.quote: וּבֵיהּ שֵׂעָר סֻמָּק דַּעְדָּק
sources.says: Onkelos translates the hair as red (סומק) and thin.

sources.quote: צהוב. בלשון ישמעאל קרוב מעין הלובן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says that in Arabic צהוב is a color close to white.

13:45.headline: פרוע: hair grown wild, or a head covered differently?
13:45.body: Rashi says פרוע means the hair is left to grow long. Ralbag says the word has two uses, uncut hair or a change in how the head is covered, and argues for the second here, since the rule starts the moment the person is declared impure.

sources.quote: פרוע. מְגֻדַּל שֵׂעָר
sources.says: Rashi says פרוע means with grown-out hair.

sources.ref: Ralbag Beur HaMilot on Torah, Leviticus 13:45:2
sources.quote: ראוי שתדע כי פריעת הראש תאמר בפנים שונים
sources.says: Ralbag says the phrase is used in different senses: hair left uncut, or the usual head covering changed.

sources.ref: Ralbag Beur HaMilot on Torah, Leviticus 13:45:2
sources.quote: והנה הרצון בזה המקום אינו לגדל פרע
sources.says: Ralbag says that here it does not mean growing the hair long.

13:46.headline: Why he sits alone: he split others apart with gossip
13:46.body: Rashi stops on בדד to ask why only this impure person must live alone. He quotes the sages: his gossip split husband from wife and friend from friend, so he is split off too.

sources.quote: הוֹאִיל וְהוּא הִבְדִּיל בְּלָשׁוֹן הָרָע בֵּין אִישׁ לְאִשְׁתּוֹ וּבֵין אִישׁ לְרֵעֵהוּ, אַף הוּא יִבָּדֵל
sources.says: Rashi says that since he separated man from wife and friend from friend with evil talk, he too is separated.

13:48.headline: שתי, the warp: the threads that are the cloth's base
13:48.body: Ibn Ezra and Chizkuni link שתי to שתות, 'foundations', since the warp is the base of the weave. Ibn Ezra says ערב, the woof, is named for mixing in with it.

sources.quote: ויתכן להיות גזרת בשתי מגזרת וחשופי שת שהוא יסוד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra suggests שתי comes from שת, meaning a foundation.

sources.quote: וטעם ערב שיתערב עם השתי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says ערב is so called because it mixes with the warp.

sources.quote: או בשתי לשון יסוד המלאכה, כמו השתות
sources.says: Chizkuni says שתי means the foundation of the work, like 'the foundations'.

13:49.headline: Does doubling a color word make it stronger or weaker?
13:49.body: Rashi and Ralbag say the doubled form ירקרק means the greenest of greens. Ibn Ezra says doubling makes it weaker, like שחרחרת, 'darkish', and notes that some say the opposite.

sources.quote: ירקרק. יָרֹק שֶׁבַּיְרֻקִּין
sources.says: Rashi says ירקרק is the greenest of greens.

sources.ref: Ralbag Beur HaMilot on Torah, Leviticus 13:49:1
sources.quote: מפני שההכפל בכל העניינים הוא לחזק הנה ירצה בזה ירוק מאד
sources.says: Ralbag says doubling always strengthens, so it means very green.

sources.quote: וזה כפול לחסרון וכן שחרחר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the doubling is for lessening, as in שחרחרת, though some say the reverse.

13:51.headline: ממארת: a stinging sore, or a curse on the cloth?
13:51.body: Rashi reads it like סלון ממאיר in Ezekiel, a pricking thorn, and gives the midrash that hears מארה, 'curse'. Ibn Ezra rejects the curse reading, but Ramban says the curse is the true sense.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן סִלּוֹן מַמְאִיר
sources.says: Rashi compares 'a pricking thorn' in Ezekiel.

sources.quote: וּמִדְרָשׁוֹ: תֵּן בּוֹ מְאֵרָה שֶׁלֹא תֵהָנֶה הֵימֶנּוּ
sources.says: Rashi gives the midrash: put a curse on it, so you get no benefit from it.

sources.quote: והמ״ם הב׳‎ במלת ממארת שורש ואינה מגזרת מארה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the second מ is part of the root, so the word does not come from מארה, curse.

sources.quote: וְהָאֱמֶת שֶׁהוּא לְשׁוֹן מְאֵרָה, כְּלוֹמַר שֶׁהִיא קִלְלַת אֱלֹהִים בַּבֶּגֶד וּבַבַּיִת
sources.says: Ramban says the truth is that it means curse: God's curse on the garment and the house.

13:55.headline: Bald spots on a garment: its worn side and its new side
13:55.body: קרחת and גבחת mean baldness at the back and front of the head. Rashi and Onkelos say that on cloth they mean the worn part and the new part, and Rashi says the Torah chose these words so the rule for people carries over to cloth.

sources.quote: קָרַחַת לְשׁוֹן יְשָׁנִים וְגַבַּחַת לְשׁוֹן חֲדָשִׁים
sources.says: Rashi says that here קרחת means old and גבחת means new.

sources.quote: לְכָךְ אָחַז הַכָּתוּב לְשׁוֹן קָרַחַת וְגַבַּחַת
sources.says: Rashi says the Torah used these words so a rule could be learned from people to garments.

sources.quote: בְּשְׁחִיקוּתֵיהּ אוֹ בְחַדָּתוּתֵיהּ
sources.says: Onkelos translates 'in its worn part or in its new part'.

13:58.headline: The same verb means 'whiten' all chapter, except here
13:58.body: Rashi notes that Onkelos translates every washing in this passage as 'whitening', but this one as 'immersing'. This second washing is a dip in water to make the cloth pure.

sources.quote: תַּרְגּוּם שֶׁל כִּבּוּסִין שֶׁבְּפָרָשָׁה זוֹ לְשׁוֹן לִבּוּן
sources.says: Rashi says Onkelos renders the washings in this passage as whitening, except this one, which means immersion.

sources.quote: דִּי יִתְחַוַּר וְיֶעְדֵּי מִנְּהוֹן מַכְתָּשָׁא וְיִצְטַבַּע תִּנְיָנוּת
sources.says: Onkelos uses 'whitened' for the first washing and 'immersed' for the second.

14:2.headline: He is 'brought' to the priest, yet the priest goes out
14:2.body: The next verse has the priest go out of the camp, so how is the leper brought to him? Ramban says it means he must come without delay, even against his will, while Chizkuni says only the news of his healing is brought in.

sources.quote: שלא ישהה. ואם כן יאמר כי ביום שיטהר שיתרפא מנגעו יובא על כרחו אל הכהן
sources.says: Ramban, following the Sifra, says he must not delay, and on the day he heals he is brought to the priest even against his will.

sources.quote: והובא דבר טהרתו אל הכהן, אבל המצורע עצמו אסור ליכנס במחנה
sources.says: Chizkuni says the matter of his cleansing is brought to the priest, since the leper himself may not enter the camp.

14:3.headline: 'The plague was healed from the leper': backwards, or exactly right?
14:3.body: We would expect 'the leper was healed from the plague'. The grammarian Yonah ibn Janah said the words are reversed, and Ibn Ezra objects that we should not reverse God's words because of our own lack of knowledge.

sources.quote: כי נרפא נגע הצרעת מן הצרוע הוא הפוך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports Rabbi Yonah's view that 'the plague was healed from the leper' is reversed.

sources.quote: ולמה נהפוך דברי אלהים חיים בעבור חוסר דעתנו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra asks why we should reverse the words of the living God because of our lack of knowledge.

14:4.headline: Why birds? Chattering for chatter
14:4.body: Rashi says the plague comes for gossip, so the cure uses birds, which chatter all the time. Ramban objects that many birds make no sound, and says צפור means small birds that sing in the early morning, from the Aramaic צפרא, morning.

sources.quote: לפי שהנגעים באין על לשון הרע שהוא מעשה פטפוטי דברים
sources.says: Rashi says the plagues come for evil speech, which is idle chatter.

sources.quote: צפרים שמפטפטין תמיד בצפצוף קול
sources.says: Rashi says birds are used because they chatter all the time.

sources.quote: כי עופות רבים אין בהם פוצה פה ומצפצף
sources.says: Ramban objects that many birds do not open their mouths to chirp.

sources.quote: ששם צפור כלל לעופות הקטנים המשכימים בבקר לצפצף ולשורר, מלשון ארמית "צפרא
sources.says: Ramban says צפור names small birds that rise early to chirp and sing, from the Aramaic word for morning.

14:4.headline: From the tall cedar to the low hyssop
14:4.body: Ibn Ezra says the cedar and the hyssop stand for the largest and smallest plants. Rashi reads a lesson: the plague comes for pride, and the cure is to make oneself low like the worm and the hyssop.

sources.quote: הוא הגדול וקטן במיני הצמחים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they are the largest and the smallest of plants.

sources.quote: לפי שהנגעים באין על גסות הרוח
sources.says: Rashi says the cedar is used because the plagues come for arrogance.

sources.quote: ישפיל עצמו מגאותו כתולעת וכאזוב
sources.says: Rashi says the cure is to lower himself from his pride like a worm and a hyssop.

14:8.headline: 'Outside his tent' means apart from his wife
14:8.body: He is already back inside the camp, yet must stay outside his tent for seven days. Rashi, from the Sifra, says this teaches that he may not be with his wife in that week.

sources.quote: וישב מחוץ לאהלו. מלמד שאסור בתשמיש המטה
sources.says: Rashi says 'outside his tent' teaches that marital relations are forbidden to him.

14:14.headline: A part of the ear even Rashi could not name
14:14.body: Rashi says תנוך is the middle ridge of the ear, but admits he does not know where the word comes from. Onkelos simply says 'the top of the ear'.

sources.quote: גדר אמצעי שבאזן, ולשון תנוך לא נודע לי
sources.says: Rashi says it is the middle ridge of the ear, and the word תנוך is unknown to him.

sources.quote: על רום אודנא דמדכי דימינא
sources.says: Onkelos translates it as the top of the right ear.

14:34.headline: A plague in the house, given as good news
14:34.body: Rashi says this was good news: the Amorites had hidden gold in their walls, and tearing down the house would uncover it. Ramban says 'I will put' shows it comes from God's hand, not nature.

sources.quote: בשורה היא להם שהנגעים באים עליהם
sources.says: Rashi says it is good news for them that the plagues come.

sources.quote: לפי שהטמינו אמוריים מטמוניות של זהב בקירות בתיהם
sources.says: Rashi says the Amorites hid treasures of gold in the walls of their houses.

sources.quote: לרמז כי יד ה' תעשה זאת לא טבע כלל
sources.says: Ramban says it hints that God's hand does this, not nature at all.

14:35.headline: 'Something like a plague': no one rules before the priest
14:35.body: The owner does not say 'a plague', only 'something like a plague'. Rashi says even a learned owner who is sure must not decide; only the priest rules.

sources.quote: שאפלו הוא חכם ויודע שהוא נגע ודאי, לא יפסק דבר ברור
sources.says: Rashi says even if he is wise and knows it is surely a plague, he should not state it as certain.

14:35.headline: The owner who keeps his house to himself
14:35.body: The verse calls him 'the one whose house is his'. Rabbeinu Bahya cites the sages: this is someone who keeps his house only for himself, will not lend tools or take in guests, and the plague comes for that meanness.

sources.quote: מי שמיוחד ביתו לו, כלומר שאינו רוצה להשאיל כלים או שאינו מכניס אורחים לביתו
sources.says: Bahya says it means one whose house is only for himself: he will not lend things or bring guests into his home.

sources.quote: שהנגעים באים על צרות העין
sources.says: Bahya says the plagues come for stinginess.

14:40.headline: 'They' pull out the stones: the neighbor pays too
14:40.body: Chizkuni says the plural teaches that the owner and his neighbor both pull out the stones, since they share the wall. From here comes the saying: woe to the wicked and woe to his neighbor.

sources.quote: מלמד ששניהם חולצים מכאן אמרו אוי לרשע אוי לשכינו
sources.says: Chizkuni says both of them remove the stones, and from here they said: woe to the wicked, woe to his neighbor.

sources.quote: לפי שהוא ושכנו שניהם חייבים בהוצאה ושותפים בבנין
sources.says: Bahya says the plural is used because he and his neighbor share the cost and the building.

18:3.headline: Their statutes here means customs, like theaters and stadiums
18:3.body: Rashi asks what this phrase adds, and answers that חקות here means their customs, things fixed for them, such as theaters and stadiums. Onkelos also translates it as their customs.

sources.quote: אֵלּוּ נִימוֹסוֹת שֶׁלָּהֶן — דְּבָרִים הַחֲקוּקִין לָהֶם — כְּגוֹן טַרְטִיָּאוֹת וְאִצְטַדִיָּאוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says these are their customs, things fixed for them, such as theaters and stadiums.

sources.quote: וּבְנִימוֹסֵיהוֹן לָא תְהָכוּן
sources.says: Onkelos translates: do not walk in their customs.

18:5.headline: Live by them: in the next world, and not die by them
18:5.body: Rashi reads וחי בהם, he shall live by them, as life in the world to come, since in this world everyone dies. Bahya gives the sages' other lesson: live by them and not die by them, so the commandments give way to saving a life.

sources.quote: וחי בהם. לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, שֶׁאִם תֹּאמַר בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וַהֲלֹא סוֹפוֹ הוּא מֵת
sources.says: Rashi says it means life in the world to come, since in this world he dies in the end.

sources.quote: וחי בהם ולא שימות בהם, שהרי המצות נדחות מפני פקוח נפש
sources.says: Bahya says, from the sages, live by them and not die by them, since the commandments are set aside to save a life.

sources.quote: וְיֵחֵי בְהוֹן לְחַיֵּי עָלְמָא
sources.says: Onkelos translates: he will live by them in eternal life.

18:6.headline: Come near: a modest word, and a plural that includes women
18:6.body: Ibn Ezra says do not come near is a polite way to say lying together. Rashi says the verb is plural so that it warns women as well as men.

sources.quote: לא תקרבו. כנוי לשכיבה וכן ואקרב אל הנביאה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says do not come near is a polite word for lying together, as in I came near to the prophetess.

sources.quote: לְהַזְהִיר הַנְּקֵבָה כַּזָּכָר, לְכָךְ נֶאֱמַר לְשׁוֹן רַבִּים
sources.says: Rashi says it is in the plural to warn the woman as well as the man.

18:7.headline: Your father's nakedness: his wife, or your mother herself
18:7.body: Rashi, from the Talmud, reads your father's nakedness as your father's wife, learned from a later verse. Bahya gives the plain sense: it is one law, since uncovering your mother is uncovering your father.

sources.quote: ערות אביך. זוֹ אֵשֶׁת אָבִיךָ
sources.says: Rashi says your father's nakedness means your father's wife.

sources.quote: הכל לאו אחד, ובאור הכתוב לא תגלה ערות אמך שאם עשית כן אתה מגלה ערות אביך
sources.says: Bahya says in the plain sense it is all one prohibition: do not uncover your mother, because if you do, you uncover your father.

18:17.headline: זמה: a sinful plan, a lewd thought, or what is this?
18:17.body: Rashi reads זמה as counsel, since your impulse advises you to sin. Ramban objects that this is true of every sin, and ties זמה to זמם, to plot, so it is lust carried out in thought; Bekhor Shor cites the rabbis' play זו מה, what is she worth more than another woman?

sources.quote: זמה. עֵצָה, כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ עֲצַת חֶטְאִין, שֶׁיִּצְרְךָ יוֹעֶצְךָ לַחֲטֹא
sources.says: Rashi says זמה means counsel, as Onkelos has it, a counsel of sins, because your impulse advises you to sin.

sources.quote: וְלֹא יָדַעְתִּי טַעַם לָזֶה, שֶׁכָּל הָעֲרָיוֹת, גַּם הָעֲבֵרוֹת הָאֲחֵרוֹת, הַיֵּצֶר יוֹעֲצוֹ לַחְטֹא
sources.says: Ramban says he does not see the point, since for every forbidden union and every other sin the impulse gives counsel.

sources.quote: כִּי שֵׁם "זִמָּה" גָּזְרוּ מִן "כַּאֲשֶׁר זָמַם לַעֲשׂוֹת לְאָחִיו"
sources.says: Ramban says the word זמה comes from as he plotted to do to his brother.

sources.quote: וְלַזְּנוּת הֶעָשׂוּי בְּמַחְשָׁבָה בַּסֵּתֶר יִקָּרֵא "זִמָּה"
sources.says: Ramban says lust carried out in secret thought is called זמה.

sources.quote: וכן זימה פרשו זו מה היא שוה יותר מאשה אחרת שאתה נכשל בה
sources.says: Bekhor Shor says the rabbis read זמה as זו מה: what is this one worth more than another woman, that you stumble over her?

18:18.headline: Do not make sisters into rival wives
18:18.body: Rashi reads לצרר as from צרה, a rival wife: making one sister the other's rival. Ramban says this is the reason for the law, since sisters should love each other, and Chizkuni reads it as binding them both, like living widows.

sources.quote: לצרר. לְשׁוֹן צָרָה — לַעֲשׂוֹת אֶת זוֹ צָרָה לָזוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says לצרר comes from צרה, rival wife: to make one a rival to the other.

sources.quote: כִּי הֵן רְאוּיוֹת שֶׁתִּהְיֶינָה אוֹהֲבוֹת זוֹ אֶת זוֹ, לֹא שֶׁתִּהְיֶינָה צָרוֹת
sources.says: Ramban says sisters should love one another, not be rival wives.

sources.quote: אל תגרום שתהיינה שתיהן צרורות בחייהן אלמנות חיות
sources.says: Chizkuni says do not cause both to be bound in their lifetimes like living widows.

18:20.headline: Why say for seed? Even for children it is forbidden
18:20.body: Ibn Ezra reads לזרע as even for having children, so a neighbor's wife is forbidden in every way. Ramban adds that the word may give the reason: no one would know whose child it is.

sources.quote: ואחר שאמר הכתוב לזרע שטעמו אפילו לזרע הנה היא אסורה אסור חמור
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says that since the verse says for seed, meaning even for seed, she is strictly forbidden.

sources.quote: לְהַזְכִּיר טַעַם הָאִסּוּר, כִּי לֹא יִוָּדַע הַזֶּרַע לְמִי הוּא
sources.says: Ramban says it may give the reason for the law: it would not be known whose child it is.

18:21.headline: Molech: an idol's name, or anything you make your king
18:21.body: Rashi says Molech was an idol by that name, worshipped by passing a child between two fires. Ibn Ezra cites the sages that it is a general name for anything a person makes king over himself, and Bahya says the name comes from kingship.

sources.quote: הִיא שֶׁשְּׁמָהּ מֹלֶךְ, וְזוֹ הִיא עֲבוֹדָתָהּ
sources.says: Rashi says it is an idol whose name is Molech, and he describes how it was worshipped.

sources.quote: וּמַעֲבִירִין אֶת הַבֵּן בְּרַגְלָיו בֵּין שְׁתֵּי מְדוּרוֹת הָאֵשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says they passed the son on foot between two fires.

sources.quote: למלך. שם צלם ודרשו חז״ל שהוא שם כלל כל מי שימליכנו עליו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the name of an image, and the sages taught it is a general name for whatever a person makes king over himself.

sources.quote: ונקראת מולך מלשון מלכות ואדנות
sources.says: Bahya says it is called Molech from the words for kingship and lordship.

18:22.headline: תועבה heard as you go astray in it
18:22.body: Bekhor Shor cites the rabbis' reading of תועבה, abomination, as תועה אתה בה, you go astray through it. Ibn Ezra says it is called this because it is loathsome to a holy soul.

sources.quote: וכן תועבה תועה אתה בה
sources.says: Bekhor Shor says the rabbis read תועבה as you go astray in it.

sources.quote: והזכיר תועבה היא. כי הוא דבר נתעב לנפש קדושה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is called תועבה because it is loathsome to a holy soul.

18:23.headline: תבל: a mixing of kinds, or what spice is in it?
18:23.body: Rashi reads תבל as a word for lewdness, or as a mixing of human and animal seed. Bekhor Shor cites the rabbis' play on תבלין, spice: what flavor could anyone find in so ugly a sin?

sources.quote: תבל הוא. לְשׁוֹן קָדֵשׁ וְעֶרְוָה וְנִאוּף
sources.says: Rashi says תבל is a word for lewdness and adultery.

sources.quote: דָּבָר אַחֵר תֶּבֶל הוּא לְשׁוֹן בְּלִילָה וְעִרְבּוּב זֶרַע אָדָם וְזֶרַע בְּהֵמָה
sources.says: Rashi's second reading: it means mixing human seed with animal seed.

sources.quote: וכי תבלין יש בה בעברה מכוערת זו שאתה מוצא בה טעם
sources.says: Bekhor Shor cites the rabbis: is there spice in this ugly sin, that you find flavor in it?

18:28.headline: The land is like a prince who cannot keep bad food down
18:28.body: Rashi compares the land to a prince fed something disgusting, which his stomach throws up. Onkelos translates the verb as emptying: the land empties itself of them.

sources.quote: מָשָׁל לְבֶן מֶלֶךְ שֶׁהֶאֱכִילוּהוּ דָּבָר מָאוּס, שֶׁאֵין עוֹמֵד בְּמֵעָיו אֶלָּא מְקִיאוֹ
sources.says: Rashi gives a parable of a king's son fed something disgusting, which does not stay in his stomach but he vomits it.

sources.quote: כָּךְ אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵינָהּ מְקַיֶּמֶת עוֹבְרֵי עֲבֵרָה
sources.says: Rashi says so the land of Israel does not keep those who sin.

sources.quote: וְתַרְגּוּמוֹ וְלָא תְרוֹקֵן, לְשׁוֹן רִקּוּן — מְרִיקָה עַצְמָהּ מֵהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says Onkelos translates it as emptying: the land empties itself of them.

19:2.headline: What 'be holy' asks: avoiding the forbidden, or restraint in the allowed?
19:2.body: Rashi says 'be holy' means keep away from forbidden relations. Ramban says it means restraint even in what is allowed, since a person can overindulge in food, wine and sex and be a scoundrel with the Torah's permission.

sources.quote: הוו פרושים מן העריות ומן העברה
sources.says: Rashi says: keep apart from forbidden relations and from sin.

sources.quote: והנה יהיה נבל ברשות התורה
sources.says: Ramban says a person could be a scoundrel with the Torah's permission.

sources.quote: שנהיה פרושים מן המתרות
sources.says: Ramban says the command is to hold back from things that are permitted.

19:3.headline: Here the mother comes first
19:3.body: In the Ten Commandments the father comes first; here the mother does. Rashi says a child naturally fears his father more and honors his mother more, so each verse puts first the parent who needs it.

sources.quote: כאן הקדים אם לאב, לפי שגלוי לפניו שהבן ירא את אביו יותר מאמו
sources.says: Rashi says the mother is put first here because God knows a child fears his father more than his mother.

19:4.headline: Idols named 'nothings'
19:4.body: Rashi hears אל, 'not', in אלילים: idols count as nothing. Ibn Ezra says the name means falsehood, as in Job's 'worthless healers'.

sources.quote: אלילים לשון אל — כלא הוא חשוב
sources.says: Rashi says אלילים comes from אל, 'not': they are counted as nothing.

sources.quote: ונקראו כן כי הם דבר שקר כמו רופאי אליל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they are called this because they are a lie, as in 'worthless healers'.

19:5.headline: An offering 'for your acceptance', or 'by your own will'?
19:5.body: Rashi reads it as 'so that it will be accepted for you': slaughter it with the right intent, or it will not be accepted. Ibn Ezra reads 'by your own will': bring it freely, not under pressure.

sources.quote: תחלת זביחתו תהא על מנת נחת רוח — שיהא לכם לרצון
sources.says: Rashi says the slaughter must be done so that it will be accepted for you.

sources.quote: שיביאו הזבח ברצונם ולא בהכרח
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they should bring the offering willingly, not by force.

19:10.headline: Baby grape clusters left for the poor
19:10.body: Rashi says עוללות are small, poorly formed clusters, with no shoulder and no hanging tip. Rabbeinu Bahya says they are named after עולל, a small child, since they are to a full cluster as a child is to a man.

sources.quote: כל שאין לו לא כתף ולא נטף
sources.says: Rashi says it is any cluster that has neither a shoulder nor a hanging tip.

sources.quote: ונקראו עוללות לפי שהן לשאר האשכולות כעולל לאיש
sources.says: Bahya says they are called עוללות because they are to other clusters as a small child is to a man.

19:10.headline: Single fallen grapes, like single plucked notes
19:10.body: פרט, found only here, means single grapes that drop during the harvest. Ibn Ezra links it to the word Amos uses for plucking at a harp, one note at a time.

sources.quote: גרגרי ענבים הנושרים בשעת בצירה
sources.says: Rashi says these are single grapes that fall during the grape harvest.

sources.quote: מגזרת הפורטים על פי הנבל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it comes from the root of 'those who pluck upon the harp'.

19:14.headline: Why forbid cursing someone who cannot hear it?
19:14.body: Rabbeinu Bahya says if you may not curse someone who cannot even hear it, surely not one who can. The ban is about the curser's own character, not the hurt to the listener.

sources.quote: אם החרש שלא ישמע כשהוא מקלל אותו הזהירה עליו תורה אין צ"ל מי שישמע
sources.says: Bahya says if the Torah warns about the deaf man who does not hear the curse, all the more one who hears.

sources.quote: ואין האיסור מצד חברו השומע אלא מצד עצמו
sources.says: Bahya says the ban is not because of the listener but because of the speaker himself.

19:14.headline: The 'blind' person is anyone who cannot see the trap
19:14.body: Rashi reads 'blind' as anyone blind to a matter: do not give someone advice that harms him, telling him to sell his field so you can take it. Bekhor Shor adds handing wine to a nazirite, who could not sin without you.

sources.quote: לפני הסומא בדבר לא תתן עצה שאינה הוגנת לו
sources.says: Rashi says: before one who is blind in a matter, do not give advice that is not good for him.

sources.quote: כגון מושיט כוס יין לנזיר
sources.says: Bekhor Shor gives the example of handing a cup of wine to a nazirite.

19:15.headline: Do not favor the poor, not even out of pity
19:15.body: פנים usually means face, but Maimonides says here it means favor. Rashi explains: do not rule for a poor man thinking the rich one owes him charity anyway.

sources.quote: פנים הוא גם שם החסות וההשגחה: "לא תשא פני דל
sources.says: Maimonides says פנים also means favor and care, as in 'do not favor the poor'.

sources.quote: שלא תאמר עני הוא זה, והעשיר חיב לפרנסו
sources.says: Rashi says: do not say, this man is poor and the rich man must support him anyway.

19:15.headline: Judge fairly, and judge people favorably
19:15.body: Plainly, the verse tells a judge to rule fairly. Rashi adds a second reading for everyone: judge each person favorably, giving them the benefit of the doubt.

sources.quote: כמשמעו; ד"א: הוי דן את חברך לכף זכות
sources.says: Rashi says it means what it says, and also: judge your fellow on the side of merit.

19:16.headline: The gossip as a peddler going house to house
19:16.body: Rashi says gossips are called רכיל because they go about spying, from רגל, foot, with כ and ג trading places, and a peddler, רוכל, also goes house to house. Ibn Ezra says the gossip is like a peddler: he takes from one and passes it to another.

sources.quote: נקראים הולכי רכיל — הולכי רגילה
sources.says: Rashi says they are called 'goers of רכיל', goers of spying.

sources.quote: שהכ"ף נחלפת בגימ"ל
sources.says: Rashi says the letter כ swaps with ג.

sources.quote: כי הרוכל מעתיק יקנה מזה וימכור לזה והרכיל יגלה לזה מה ששמע מזה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the peddler buys from one and sells to another, and the gossip tells one what he heard from another.

19:16.headline: Do not stand by, or do not stand with killers?
19:16.body: Rashi reads it as 'do not stand by' while your neighbor dies and you could save him, as when he is drowning. Ibn Ezra, reading it with the ban on gossip, says 'do not join killers', since many were killed because of informers.

sources.quote: לראות במיתתו ואתה יכול להצילו, כגון טובע בנהר
sources.says: Rashi says: do not watch him die when you can save him, as when he is drowning in a river.

sources.quote: שלא יתחבר עם אנשי דמים וידוע כי כמה נרצחו ונהרגו בעבור המלשינות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says do not join men of blood, for many were killed because of informing.

19:17.headline: Rebuke him, but whose sin do you carry?
19:17.body: Rashi reads 'do not bear sin because of him' as: when you rebuke him, do not shame him in public. Ramban reads it as: if you do not rebuke him, you share the guilt for his sin.

sources.quote: לא תלבין את פניו ברבים
sources.says: Rashi says: do not embarrass him in public.

sources.quote: שיהיה עליך אשם כאשר יחטא ולא הכחת אותו
sources.says: Ramban says guilt will be on you when he sins and you did not rebuke him.

19:18.headline: Revenge and grudge: the sickle and the axe
19:18.body: Rashi gives the classic example. Refusing to lend your axe because he would not lend you his sickle is revenge; lending it while saying 'I am not like you' is bearing a grudge.

sources.quote: אמר לו איני משאילך כדרך שלא השאלתני, זו היא נקימה
sources.says: Rashi says: if he answers, I will not lend to you just as you did not lend to me, that is revenge.

sources.quote: אמר לו הא לך, איני כמותך שלא השאלתני, זו היא נטירה
sources.says: Rashi says: if he answers, here it is, I am not like you who would not lend to me, that is bearing a grudge.

19:18.headline: Love your neighbor exactly as yourself? Ramban says that is impossible
19:18.body: Rabbi Akiva calls this a great rule of the Torah. Ramban says no heart can love another exactly as itself, so it means wanting every good for your friend as you want it for yourself, without envy.

sources.quote: אמר רבי עקיבא זה כלל גדול בתורה
sources.says: Rashi quotes Rabbi Akiva: this is a great rule in the Torah.

sources.quote: הפלגה, כי לא יקבל לב האדם שיאהב את חברו כאהבתו את נפשו
sources.says: Ramban says it is an overstatement, since the human heart cannot love another as much as itself.

sources.quote: שיאהב הטוב לחברו כמו לנפשו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means to love the good for his fellow as for himself.

19:19.headline: Laws with no reason, or laws with a hidden reason?
19:19.body: Rashi says חקים are a king's decrees with no reason given. Ramban says every law of God has a reason, only hidden, and here God made each kind of creature to breed after its own kind.

sources.quote: חקים — אלו גזרת מלך שאין טעם לדבר
sources.says: Rashi says חקים are royal decrees with no reason.

sources.quote: ואין הכונה בהם שתהיה גזרת מלך מלכי המלכים בשום מקום בלא טעם
sources.says: Ramban says this does not mean any decree of the King of kings lacks a reason.

sources.quote: כי השם ברא המינים בעולם
sources.says: Ramban says the reason is that God created the separate kinds in the world.

19:19.headline: A word the sages split into three
19:19.body: The sages, quoted by Rashi, split שעטנז into three words: combed smooth, spun, and twisted together. Ibn Ezra notes the word stands alone in Scripture.

sources.quote: דבר שהוא שוע טווי ונוז
sources.says: Rashi says it is something smoothed, spun and twisted.

sources.quote: המעתיקים אמרו שהיא שלש מלות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the bearers of tradition said it is three words.

sources.quote: והוא שם לבדו במקרא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word stands alone in Scripture.

19:20.headline: A word even Rashi had no parallel for
19:20.body: Rashi says it means designated for a man, and admits he knows no other example in Scripture. Ibn Ezra hears חרפה, shame, since she is a servant, while Ramban hears חרף, youth: she is a young woman attached to a man.

sources.quote: מיעדת ומיחדת לאיש, ואיני יודע לו דמיון במקרא
sources.says: Rashi says it means designated for a man, and he knows no parallel in Scripture.

sources.quote: שהמלה מגזרת חרפה בעבור היותה שפחה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word comes from חרפה, shame, because she is a servant.

sources.quote: ויקראו ימי הנעורים ימי חרף
sources.says: Ramban says the days of youth are called the days of חרף.

19:23.headline: A tree's fruit called 'uncircumcised'
19:23.body: ערלה usually means foreskin. Rashi reads it here as 'sealed off': the young tree's fruit is closed to use, and Ramban compares an 'uncircumcised heart', a closed heart.

sources.quote: ואטמתם אטימתו — יהא אטום ונסתם מלהנות ממנו
sources.says: Rashi says it means you shall seal it off: it is closed and blocked from any use.

sources.quote: ואם כן יהיה "ערל לב" (יחזקאל מד ט) - סגור לב
sources.says: Ramban says an uncircumcised heart means a closed heart.

19:25.headline: The Torah answers the farmer's complaint
19:25.body: Rabbi Akiva says the Torah speaks to a person's natural worry: 'four years I have worked on this tree for nothing'. So it promises that keeping the law will increase the fruit.

sources.quote: היה רבי עקיבא אומר דברה תורה כנגד יצר הרע
sources.says: Rashi quotes Rabbi Akiva: the Torah spoke against the evil inclination.

sources.quote: שלא יאמר אדם הרי ארבע שנים אני מצטער בו חנם
sources.says: Rashi says it is so a person will not say, four years I have toiled over it for nothing.

19:26.headline: Eating 'on the blood': a meal shared with demons
19:26.body: 'Do not eat on the blood' is read many ways. Maimonides says idolaters ate meat around a pit of blood to share a meal with demons and learn the future, while Rashbam says they ate on a murdered man's grave so he would not be avenged.

sources.quote: להרבה פנים נדרש בסנהדרין
sources.says: Rashi says the verse is expounded in many ways in Sanhedrin.

sources.quote: היו שוחטים חיה ואוספים את דמה בכלי או בגומה, והיו אוכלים את בשרה של הנשחטת סביב אותו דם
sources.says: Maimonides says they would slaughter an animal, collect its blood in a vessel or pit, and eat the meat around that blood.

sources.quote: שאוכלים על קבר ההרוג לשם מכשפות שלא ינקום
sources.says: Rashbam says they ate on the grave of a murdered man, as sorcery, so he would not take revenge.

19:26.headline: Lucky days, or reading the clouds?
19:26.body: Rashi reads it from עונות, times: saying one day is lucky to start work, or one hour bad to set out. Ibn Ezra reads it from ענן, cloud: reading omens in the shapes and motion of clouds.

sources.quote: לשון עונות ושעות, שאומר יום פלוני יפה להתחיל מלאכה
sources.says: Rashi says it means times and hours: saying such a day is good to begin work.

sources.quote: והנכון בעיני מגזרת ענן כי ידוע כי יש מי שיעונן שיסתכל בעננים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it comes from ענן, cloud, for some look at clouds to read omens.

19:28.headline: Here נפש means a dead body
19:28.body: נפש usually means a soul or a living person. Ibn Ezra and Onkelos say here it means the dead, and Rashi explains that the Amorites cut their flesh when someone died.

sources.quote: ומלת לנפש. הגוף המת וכן מתורגם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says לנפש means the dead body, as the Aramaic translates.

sources.quote: וחבול על מית
sources.says: Onkelos translates: a cut for the dead.

sources.quote: כן דרכן של אמוריים להיות משרטין בשרם כשמת להם מת
sources.says: Rashi says this was the way of the Amorites, to cut their flesh when someone died.

19:29.headline: When the land itself 'strays'
19:29.body: Rashi says the land itself will 'stray': it will give its fruit elsewhere and hold back rain from you. Ibn Ezra says 'the land' just means the people of the land.

sources.quote: הארץ מזנה את פרותיה לעשותן במקום אחר ולא בארצכם
sources.says: Rashi says the land will stray with its fruit, giving it somewhere else and not in your land.

sources.quote: הטעם זנות אנשי הארץ
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means the straying of the people of the land.

19:29.headline: Lewdness read as 'who is this one?'
19:29.body: Chizkuni splits זמה, lewdness, into זו מה, 'what is this one?'. Bekhor Shor explains: when no one knows whose child a woman carries, a father may end up with his own daughter.

sources.quote: זמה זו מה היא
sources.says: Chizkuni reads זמה as 'this one, what is she?'.

sources.quote: שאינה יודעת ממי מתעברת ונמצא אב בא על בתו
sources.says: Bekhor Shor says she does not know by whom she conceived, and so a father may come to his own daughter.

19:31.headline: The medium who speaks from the armpit
19:31.body: Rashi says a בעל אוב is a medium whose voice seems to come from his armpit. Ibn Ezra links the word to אובות, the wineskins of Job, which he says are central to the trick.

sources.quote: בעל אוב זה פיתום המדבר משחיו
sources.says: Rashi says a בעל אוב is a medium who speaks from his armpit.

sources.quote: האבת. מגזרת וכאובות חדשים כי הם עיקר זאת האומנות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word comes from 'like new wineskins', since they are the heart of this craft.

19:32.headline: An 'elder' is one who has acquired wisdom
19:32.body: The sages read זקן, elder, as one who has acquired wisdom, so the verse honors the learned, even the young. Ramban adds that the law follows Isi ben Yehuda: every old person is honored too.

sources.quote: אין זקן אלא שקנה חכמה
sources.says: Rashi says an elder is only one who has acquired wisdom.

sources.quote: איסי בן יהודה אומר כל שיבה במשמע
sources.says: Ramban cites Isi ben Yehuda: every old person is meant.

sources.quote: מן קדם דסבר באוריתא תקום
sources.says: Onkelos translates: rise before one who is wise in Torah.

19:33.headline: Wronging a convert with words
19:33.body: Rashi says this is wronging with words. Do not tell a convert: yesterday you worshipped idols, and now you come to learn the Torah given by God.

sources.quote: אונאת דברים; לא תאמר לו אמש היית עובד ע"ז
sources.says: Rashi says it means wronging with words: do not say to him, yesterday you worshipped idols.

19:35.headline: A shopkeeper's measure counts as a court of law
19:35.body: The verse repeats 'do no wrong in judgment' and then lists measures and weights. Rashi says one who measures is called a judge, so cheating on a measure is like corrupting justice.

sources.quote: מלמד שהמודד נקרא דין, שאם שקר במדה הרי הוא כמקלקל את הדין
sources.says: Rashi says the one who measures is called a judge: if he cheats in measure, he is like one who corrupts justice.

19:36.headline: Honest weights, and the God who knew the firstborn in Egypt
19:36.body: Why mention leaving Egypt beside honest weights? Rashi says the God who could tell in Egypt which child was a firstborn can also tell who hides his weights in salt to cheat.

sources.quote: אני הבחנתי במצרים בין טפה של בכור לטפה שאינה של בכור
sources.says: Rashi says God distinguished in Egypt between the drop that made a firstborn and one that did not.

sources.quote: ואני הנאמן לפרע ממי שטומן משקלותיו במלח
sources.says: Rashi says God can be trusted to punish one who hides his weights in salt.

2:2.headline: A rare word for a handful, measured with three fingers
2:2.body: קמץ is a rare word for a handful. Rashi says it means three fingers closed over the palm, 'as the Hebrew word means'. Chizkuni explains why Rashi says Hebrew: in Aramaic the same word means a pit.

sources.quote: חופה שלוש אצבעותיו על פס ידו, וזהו קמץ במשמע לשון העברית
sources.says: Rashi says the priest bends three fingers over his palm, and that is what קמץ means in Hebrew.

sources.quote: לפי שמצינו במקום אחר קומץ כמשמע לשון גומא בלשון תרגום
sources.says: Chizkuni says Rashi stressed the Hebrew meaning because in the Aramaic translation the word means a pit.

2:7.headline: A deep pan named for the dough that quivers inside it
2:7.body: מרחשת appears only twice. Rashi says it was a deep pan where oil pooled, so the soft dough in it seemed to stir, from רחש, to move. The midrash contrasts it with the flat מחבת, where the dough comes out hard.

sources.quote: מעשי מנחה העשויין לתוכה רוחשין; כל דבר רך על ידי משקה נראה כרוחש ומנענע
sources.says: Rashi says the offering made in it quivers, since anything soft in liquid seems to stir and move.

sources.quote: ויש מפרשם מגזרת רחש לבי והטעם בעבור שישמיע קול
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports a view that links it to 'my heart stirs' (רחש לבי), because it makes a sound.

sources.quote: מרחשת עמוקה, מעשיה רוחשין. מחבת צפה, מעשיה קשין
sources.says: The midrash says the מרחשת is deep and its contents quiver, while the מחבת is flat and its contents are hard.

2:11.headline: Here 'honey' means any fruit syrup, like dates
2:11.body: דבש usually means bee honey. Rashi says any sweet juice of fruit is called דבש, and Rashbam says the fruit meant is dates. So the ban on the altar covers fruit sweeteners too.

sources.quote: כל מתיקת פרי קרויה דבש
sources.says: Rashi says all sweetness of fruit is called דבש.

sources.quote: פירות האילן תמרים קרויין דבש
sources.says: Rashbam says the tree fruit called דבש is dates.

2:14.headline: A rare word for grain cracked in a mill
2:14.body: גרש appears only twice in the Bible. Rashi reads it from גרס, to break and grind, as in 'he has broken my teeth with gravel'. Ibn Ezra adds 'my soul is crushed' (גרסה נפשי).

sources.quote: גרש לשון שבירה וטחינה, גורסה ברחים של גרוסות, כמו ויגרס בחצץ
sources.says: Rashi says גרש means breaking and grinding, done in a mill for groats, like 'he broke with gravel'.

sources.quote: וקרוב מגזרת גרסה נפשי ואם הוא בסמ״ך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is close to 'my soul is crushed', even though that word is spelled with a samekh.

20:2.headline: People of the land: the nation the earth was made for
20:2.body: Rashi reads עם הארץ as the people for whose sake the earth was created, who will inherit the land by keeping these laws. Ibn Ezra reads it simply as the people of the land where the man lives.

sources.quote: עַם שֶׁבְּגִינוֹ נִבְרֵאת הָאָרֶץ, עַם שֶׁעֲתִידִין לִירַשׁ הָאָרֶץ עַל יְדֵי מִצְווֹת הַלָּלוּ
sources.says: Rashi says it is the people for whom the earth was created, who will inherit the land through these commandments.

sources.quote: וטעם עם הארץ. ארץ שהוא דר בה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means the people of the land where he lives.

20:3.headline: My face, my free time: God drops everything for him
20:3.body: Rashi hears פני, my face, as פנאי, my free time: God turns away from all other business to deal with this man. Onkelos translates the phrase as my anger.

sources.quote: פְּנַאי שֶׁלִּי — פּוֹנֶה אֲנִי מִכָּל עֲסָקַי וְעוֹסֵק בּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it means my free time: I turn from all my business and deal with him.

sources.quote: וַאֲנָא אֶתֵּן יָת רוּגְזִי בְּגַבְרָא הַהוּא
sources.says: Onkelos translates: I will set my anger against that man.

20:4.headline: Look away once, and you will look away again and again
20:4.body: The verse doubles the verb, העלם יעלימו, if they hide their eyes. Rashi reads the doubling as a warning: ignore one thing and you will end up ignoring many, and if a small court ignores it, the great court will too.

sources.quote: אִם הֶעְלִימוּ בְּדָבָר אֶחָד, סוֹף שֶׁיַּעְלִימוּ בִדְבָרִים הַרְבֵּה
sources.says: Rashi says if they look away in one matter, in the end they will look away in many.

sources.quote: אִם הֶעְלִימוּ סַנְהֶדְרֵי קְטַנָּה, סוֹף שֶׁיַּעְלִימוּ סַנְהֶדְרֵי גְדוֹלָה
sources.says: Rashi says if a small court looks away, in the end the great court will too.

20:5.headline: Why punish the family? Because they cover for him
20:5.body: Rabbi Shimon asks what the family did wrong. Rashi gives his answer: in a family with a tax collector, all of them act like tax collectors, because they all cover for him.

sources.quote: אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעון וכִי מִשְׁפָּחָה מֶה חָטְאָה
sources.says: Rashi cites Rabbi Shimon asking what sin the family committed.

sources.quote: שֶׁאֵין לְךָ מִשְׁפָּחָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ מוֹכֵס שֶׁאֵין כֻּלָּם מוֹכְסִין — שֶׁכֻּלָּן מְחַפִּין עָלָיו
sources.says: Rashi says no family that has a tax collector is free of being tax collectors, since they all cover for him.

sources.quote: בְּגַבְרָא הַהוּא וּבִסְעָדוֹהִי
sources.says: Onkelos translates family as that man's helpers.

20:9.headline: His blood is on him: stoning, or simply his own fault
20:9.body: Rashi says the rabbis read דמיו בו as death by stoning, learned from a later verse. In the plain sense, he says, it means his blood is on his own head: he alone caused his death.

sources.quote: דמיו בו. זוֹ סְקִילָה, וְכֵן כָּל מָקוֹם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר דָּמָיו בּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it means stoning, and so wherever it says his blood is on him.

sources.quote: וּפְשׁוּטוֹ שֶׁל מִקְרָא, כְּמוֹ דָּמוֹ בְרֹאשׁוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the plain sense is like his blood is on his head.

sources.quote: שֶׁהוּא גָרַם לְעַצְמוֹ שֶׁיֵּהָרֵג
sources.says: Rashi says he brought his own death on himself.

20:14.headline: Them, or one of them? A Greek word inside ואתהן
20:14.body: ואתהן means and them, which seems to burn both women, though his first wife married him lawfully. Some rabbis, Rashi says, split it into את הן, one of them, since הן means one in Greek.

sources.quote: אֵי אַתָּה יָכוֹל לוֹמַר אִשְׁתּוֹ הָרִאשׁוֹנָה יִשְׂרְפוּ, שֶׁהֲרֵי נְשָׂאָהּ בְּהֶתֵּר
sources.says: Rashi says you cannot say his first wife is burned, since he married her lawfully.

sources.quote: וּמַהוּ אֶתְהֶן? אֶת אַחַת מֵהֶן וְלָשׁוֹן יְוָנִי הוּא הֵן אַחַת
sources.says: Rashi says some rabbis read אתהן as one of them, because in Greek הן means one.

sources.quote: ורבותינו דרשו ועשאוהו כשתי תיבות: את הן, את אחת מהן, שכן בלשון יוני קורין לאחת הינה
sources.says: Bekhor Shor says the rabbis made it two words, את הן, one of them, since in Greek one is called הינה.

20:17.headline: חסד here: a disgrace, or a kindness betrayed
20:17.body: Rashi reads חסד here as the Aramaic word for disgrace, and gives a midrash: when Cain married his sister, it was God's kindness to build the world. Ramban holds that חסד keeps its usual meaning: a brother owes his sister kindness, such as helping her marry, and he harms her instead.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן אֲרַמִּי חֶרְפָּה חִסּוּדָא
sources.says: Rashi says it is the Aramaic word for disgrace, חסודא.

sources.quote: אִם תֹּאמַר קַיִן נָשָׂא אֲחוֹתוֹ חֶסֶד עָשָׂה הַמָּקוֹם, לִבְנוֹת עוֹלָמוֹ מִמֶּנּוּ
sources.says: Rashi gives the midrash: if Cain married his sister, God did a kindness, to build the world from him.

sources.quote: וְהַנָּכוֹן בְּעֵינַי בְּמִלַּת "חֶסֶד" שֶׁהוּא כְּמַשְׁמָעוֹ
sources.says: Ramban says the right reading of חסד is its plain meaning, kindness.

sources.quote: כִּי הָיָה רָאוּי שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה עִמָּהּ הַחֶסֶד שֶׁיַּעֲשׂוּ הָאַחִים לְהַשִּׂיאָהּ לְבַעַל, וְהוּא פּוֹגֵם וְעוֹכֵר אוֹתָהּ
sources.says: Ramban says he should have done her the kindness brothers do, helping her marry, but instead he damages her.

20:18.headline: ערוה, nakedness, is really the word for uncovering
20:18.body: Rashi says הערה means he uncovered, and every use of ערוה is about uncovering. The ו in ערוה is added to make a noun, like אחוה, brotherhood, from אח.

sources.quote: הערה. גִּלָּה, וְכֵן כָּל לְשׁוֹן עֶרְוָה גִּלּוּי הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says הערה means uncovered, and every form of ערוה means uncovering.

sources.quote: וְהַוָּי"ו יוֹרֶדֶת בַּתֵּיבָה לְשֵׁם דָּבָר
sources.says: Rashi says the ו enters the word to make it a noun.

sources.quote: וְכֵן אַחֲוָה מִגִּזְרַת אָח
sources.says: Rashi gives the example of אחוה from אח.

20:20.headline: Childless: one who has children will bury them
20:20.body: Rashi and Onkelos read ערירים as without children, like Abraham's words I go childless, and Ibn Ezra rejects the Sadducees' reading of naked. Rashi says die childless means he buries any children he has, while the next verse's be childless means he never has any.

sources.quote: כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ, בְּלָא וְלָד, וְדוֹמֶה לוֹ וְאָנֹכִי הוֹלֵךְ עֲרִירִי
sources.says: Rashi says it means as the Aramaic translation has it, without a child, like I go childless.

sources.quote: יֵשׁ לוֹ בָנִים, קוֹבְרָן, אֵין לוֹ בָנִים, מֵת בְּלֹא בָנִים
sources.says: Rashi says if he has children, he buries them, and if he has none, he dies without children.

sources.quote: אמרו הצדוקים שהוא כמו ערומים ופירוש ימותו כמו יומתו ולא אמרו אמת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the Sadducees read it as naked and that they are wrong.

20:21.headline: Why a brother's wife is called נדה
20:21.body: Bahya says נדה here does not mean a woman in her period, and Rashi reads it as shunned and loathsome. Chizkuni adds a comparison: a niddah is forbidden for a time and then allowed, and a brother's wife may become allowed if he dies childless.

sources.quote: אין הכונה נדה ממש בשפע דם
sources.says: Bahya says the meaning is not an actual niddah with a flow of blood.

sources.quote: הַשְּׁכִיבָה הַזֹּאת מְנֻדָּה הִיא וּמְאוּסָה
sources.says: Rashi says this act of lying together is shunned and loathsome.

sources.quote: אף באשת אח פעמים שהיא אסורה ופעמים שהיא מותרת ע״‎י יבום כשנתאלמנה בלא זרע
sources.says: Chizkuni says a brother's wife is sometimes forbidden and sometimes allowed, through levirate marriage when she is widowed without children.

20:23.headline: God loathes them, like a man sick of his food
20:23.body: Rashi reads ואקץ as loathing, as in קצתי בחיי, I am sick of my life, like a man sick of his food. Onkelos translates it as my word kept them far, and Ibn Ezra says it is a figure of speech.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן מִאוּס, כְּמוֹ קַצְתִּי בְחַיַּי
sources.says: Rashi says it means loathing, like I am sick of my life.

sources.quote: כְּאָדָם שֶׁהוּא קָץ בִּמְזוֹנוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it is like a man who is sick of his food.

sources.quote: וְרָחִיק מֵימְרִי יָתְהוֹן
sources.says: Onkelos translates: my word kept them far away.

sources.quote: ואקץ בם. דרך משל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a figure of speech.

20:26.headline: Do not say pork disgusts you; say God forbade it
20:26.body: Rashi, from the Sifra, reads ואבדל, I set you apart, as a lesson. A person should not say I cannot stand pork, but I could, and my Father in heaven forbade it, so the separation is for God's sake.

sources.quote: מִנַּיִן שֶׁלֹּא יֹאמַר אָדָם נַפְשִׁי קָצָה בִּבְשַׂר חֲזִיר
sources.says: Rashi asks how we know a person should not say I am disgusted by pork.

sources.quote: אֲבָל יֹאמַר אֶפְשִׁי וּמָה אֶעֱשֶׂה וְאָבִי שֶׁבַּשָּׁמַיִם גָּזַר עָלַי
sources.says: Rashi says one should say I could, but what can I do, my Father in heaven forbade it.

sources.quote: שֶׁתְּהֵא הַבְדָּלַתְכֶם מֵהֶם לִשְׁמִי
sources.says: Rashi says the separation should be for God's name.

21:9.headline: Tachel: 'begins', or 'profanes herself'?
21:9.body: Ibn Ezra says many read תחל as 'begins', from תחלה. He says it comes from חלול, 'to profane'. Rashi agrees: she is profaned through harlotry.

sources.quote: לדעת רבים מגזרת תחלה ולפי דעתי מלשון חלול
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says many take it from תחלה, 'beginning', but in his view it comes from חלול, 'profaning'.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁתִּתְחַלֵּל עַ"יְ זְנוּת
sources.says: Rashi says it means when she becomes profaned through harlotry.

21:20.headline: Dak: a dwarf, or a film over the eye?
21:20.body: Ibn Ezra takes דק in its plain sense, 'thin', meaning very short. Rashi says it is a film in the eye, the same word as in Isaiah's heavens spread 'like a thin film'.

sources.quote: כן דק והוא כמשמעו להיות דק קצר קומה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says דק means what it says: thin, short of stature.

sources.quote: או דק. שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ בְעֵינָיו דֹּק, שֶׁקּוֹרִים טיל"א, כְּמוֹ "הַנּוֹטֶה כַדֹּק"
sources.says: Rashi says he has a film in his eyes, as in 'who stretches out the heavens like a film'.

21:20.headline: Yallefet: a skin disease that clings until death
21:20.body: Rashi asks why this rash is called ילפת and answers: it מלפפת, wraps around a person, until the day he dies. Ibn Ezra also reads it as clinging, from Samson who 'grasped' (וילפת) the pillars.

sources.quote: וְלָמָּה נִקְרֵאת יַלֶּפֶת? שֶׁמְּלַפֶּפֶת וְהוֹלֶכֶת עַד יוֹם הַמִּיתָה
sources.says: Rashi says it is called ילפת because it clings and stays until the day of death.

sources.quote: ילפת. כטעם דבק מגזרת וילפת שמשון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says ילפת means clinging, from 'Samson grasped' the pillars.

22:3.headline: Cut off 'from before Me' — and God is everywhere
22:3.body: One might think 'cut off from before Me' means sent away to live somewhere else. Rashi says no: the verse ends 'I am the LORD', and God is in every place, so there is nowhere to go.

sources.quote: יָכוֹל מִצַּד זֶה לְצַד זֶה — יִכָּרֵת מִמְּקוֹמוֹ וְיִתְיַשֵּׁב בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר
sources.says: Rashi raises the thought that he is cut off from one place and settles in another.

sources.quote: תַּ"ל אני ה', בְּכָל מָקוֹם אֲנִי
sources.says: Rashi answers that the verse says 'I am the LORD': I am in every place.

22:11.headline: A priest's wife eats the holy food as one 'acquired' by him
22:11.body: The verse lets a priest's purchased servant eat terumah, the priests' share of the crop. Rashi says the priest's wife may eat it from this same verse, since she too is 'acquired with his money'.

sources.quote: וְאֵשֶׁת כֹּהֵן אוֹכֶלֶת בִּתְרוּמָה מִן הַמִּקְרָא הַזֶּה, שֶׁאַף הִיא קִנְיַן כַּסְפּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says a priest's wife eats terumah because of this verse, since she too is 'acquired with his money'.

22:16.headline: 'Load them with guilt' means they load themselves
22:16.body: The verse says the priests 'cause them to bear guilt'. Rashi says אותם here means themselves, one of three places where Rabbi Yishmael read את this way.

sources.quote: אֶת עַצְמָם יִטְעֲנוּ עָוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says they will load guilt on themselves.

sources.quote: זֶה אֶחָד מִשְּׁלוֹשָׁה אֶתִים שֶׁהָיָה רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל דּוֹרֵשׁ בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁמְּדַבְּרִים בָּאָדָם עַצְמוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says this is one of three uses of את that Rabbi Yishmael read as referring to the person himself.

22:28.headline: Onkelos turns 'ox' into 'cow': the rule is about mothers
22:28.body: The law forbids killing an animal and its young on one day. The sages say it applies to a mother and her young, not a father, so Onkelos translates ושור as 'cow' and שה as 'ewe'.

sources.quote: נוֹהֵג בַּנְּקֵבָה — שֶׁאָסוּר לִשְׁחֹט הָאֵם וְהַבֵּן אוֹ הַבַּת, וְאֵינוֹ נוֹהֵג בַּזְּכָרִים
sources.says: Rashi says it applies to females: you may not slaughter the mother with her son or daughter, but it does not apply to males.

sources.quote: וזהו שתרגם אונקלוס ותורתא או שיתא, לומר שנוהג בנקבות ולא בזכרים
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says this is why Onkelos translated with the words for a cow or a ewe: the law applies to females, not males.

23:2.headline: To 'call' a festival means to fix its date
23:2.body: קרא usually means to call or proclaim. Rashbam says that with festivals it means to set a time, as in 'he has called a set time against me'.

sources.quote: כל לשון קריאה שאצל מועדים לשון קביעת זמן הוא, כמו: קרא עלי מועד
sources.says: Rashbam says every use of 'calling' with festivals means fixing a time, as in 'he called a set time against me'.

23:4.headline: Spelled so it reads 'you': the court's date holds even if wrong
23:4.body: The word for 'them' is written without a ו, so it can also be read אַתֶּם, 'you'. The sages read it as: the festivals fall when you, the court, set them, even by mistake.

sources.quote: אשר תקראו אותם. אתם כתיב, ודרשו בו אשר תקראו אתם מכאן שקדוש המועדים מסור לב"ד, ואפילו שלא בזמנו ואפילו בטעות
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says it is written אתם, read as 'you': setting the festivals is handed to the court, even off time and even in error.

sources.quote: אתם אפילו שוגגין אתם אפילו מוטעים
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya quotes the sages: 'you', even by accident; 'you', even when misled.

23:11.headline: Waving the sheaf in every direction to hold back bad weather
23:11.body: Rashi says the priest moved the offering out and back, and up and down. Out and back holds off harmful winds, and up and down holds off harmful dews.

sources.quote: מוֹלִיךְ וּמֵבִיא לַעֲצֹר רוּחוֹת רָעוֹת, מַעֲלֶה וּמוֹרִיד לַעֲצֹר טְלָלִים רָעִים
sources.says: Rashi says he moves it to and fro to stop harmful winds, and up and down to stop harmful dews.

23:16.headline: Here שבת means a week, not the Sabbath
23:16.body: In the counting of the omer, שבת stands for a whole week. Rashi follows Onkelos, who translates 'the seventh week'.

sources.quote: השבת השביעת. כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ שְׁבוּעֲתָא שְׁבִיעֵתָא
sources.says: Rashi says to read it as Onkelos does: the seventh week.

sources.quote: עַד מִבָּתַר שְׁבוּעֲתָא שְׁבִיעֵתָא
sources.says: Onkelos translates: until after the seventh week.

23:24.headline: A 'remembrance' of the shofar: what happens when the day is Sabbath
23:24.body: Rashi reads זכרון as the verses of remembrance said in prayer, recalling the ram offered in Isaac's place. Chizkuni says that when the day falls on the Sabbath the shofar is not blown, so there is only a remembrance of the blast.

sources.quote: זִכְרוֹן פְּסוּקֵי זִכְרוֹנוֹת וּפְסוּקֵי שׁוֹפָרוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says it means the verses of remembrance and the verses of the shofar.

sources.quote: לִזְכֹּר לָכֶם עֲקֵדַת יִצְחָק שֶׁקָּרַב תַּחְתָּיו אַיִל
sources.says: Rashi says this recalls the binding of Isaac, when a ram was offered in his place.

sources.quote: כשחל ראש השנה בשבת אין בו תרועה כמו שגזרו רבותינו ואין בו אלא זכרון תרועה בעלמא
sources.says: Chizkuni says that when Rosh Hashanah falls on the Sabbath there is no shofar blast, as the sages decreed, only a remembrance of it.

23:27.headline: 'But' on the tenth: the day atones only for those who return
23:27.body: In the plain sense אך means 'however'. The sages read it as a narrowing word: Yom Kippur atones for those who repent, and not for those who do not.

sources.quote: כָּל אַכִין וְרַקִּין שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה מִעוּטִים — מְכַפֵּר הוּא לַשָּׁבִים וְאֵינוֹ מְכַפֵּר עַל שֶׁאֵינָם שָׁבִים
sources.says: Rashi says every אך and רק in the Torah narrows: the day atones for those who repent, not for those who do not.

sources.quote: ע"ד הפשט כמו אמנם
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says that in the plain sense it means 'however'.

23:32.headline: Rest from evening to evening, and add a little on each side
23:32.body: Chizkuni reads 'you shall rest' as a rule for every holy day. Whether Sabbath, Yom Kippur or festival, you add some time to the rest before it starts and after it ends.

sources.quote: תשבתו כל שביתה שאתה שובת הן שבת הן יום הכיפורים הן יום טוב צריך אתה להוסיף לה בין מלפניה בין מלאחריה
sources.says: Chizkuni says every rest you keep, Sabbath, Yom Kippur or festival, needs time added both before and after.

23:40.headline: The 'beautiful' fruit is the one that 'stays' on its tree
23:40.body: הדר means beautiful, and the sages also read it as הַדָּר, 'that dwells': the etrog stays on its tree from year to year. Ibn Ezra says no fruit is more beautiful, and calls the second reading a support for the tradition.

sources.quote: הדר. הַדָּר בְּאִילָנוֹ מִשָּׁנָה לְשָׁנָה, וְזֶהוּ אֶתְרוֹג
sources.says: Rashi says הדר means it dwells on its tree from year to year, and this is the etrog.

sources.quote: עֵץ שֶׁטַּעַם עֵצוֹ וּפִרְיוֹ שָׁוֶה
sources.says: Rashi says it is a tree whose wood and fruit taste the same.

sources.quote: ובאמת כי אין פרי עץ יותר הדר ממנו ודרשו בו הדר באילנו בדרך אסמכתא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says truly no tree's fruit is more beautiful, and the reading 'dwells on its tree' is a supporting hint.

23:40.headline: A missing letter means only one palm branch
23:40.body: כפת is spelled without a ו. Rashi says the short spelling teaches that only one palm frond is taken.

sources.quote: כפת תמרים. חָסֵר וי"ו, לִמֵּד שֶׁאֵינָהּ אֶלָּא אַחַת
sources.says: Rashi says it is missing a ו, which teaches that there is only one.

24:2.headline: 'Always' here means every night, not without stopping
24:2.body: תמיד usually means always. Rashi says the lamp was lit night after night, the same way the 'always' offering was brought day after day, not burning nonstop.

sources.quote: תמיד. מִלַּיְלָה לְלַיְלָה, כְּמוֹ עוֹלַת תָּמִיד, שֶׁאֵינָהּ אֶלָּא מִיּוֹם לְיוֹם
sources.says: Rashi says תמיד means from night to night, like the daily offering called תמיד, which is only from day to day.

sources.quote: "תמיד" – אף בשבת. "תמיד" – אף בטומאה
sources.says: The Sifra reads תמיד as: even on the Sabbath, and even when the people are impure.

24:3.headline: The 'testimony' is the Ark, or the western lamp itself
24:3.body: In the plain sense the curtain of the testimony hangs before the Ark, which is called testimony. The sages read it as the western lamp of the menorah, a daily sign to the world that God's presence rests with Israel.

sources.quote: שֶׁלִּפְנֵי הָאָרוֹן שֶׁהוּא קָרוּי עֵדוּת
sources.says: Rashi says it is the curtain in front of the Ark, which is called testimony.

sources.quote: וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ דָרְשׁוּ עַל נֵר מַעֲרָבִי, שֶׁהוּא עֵדוּת לְכָל בָּאֵי עוֹלָם שֶׁהַשְּׁכִינָה שׁוֹרָה בְיִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says the sages read it as the western lamp, a testimony to everyone that the divine presence rests among Israel.

24:4.headline: The 'pure' menorah: pure gold, or freshly cleaned
24:4.body: Rashi gives two readings of הטהרה. The menorah is pure because it is made of pure gold, or because the priest first cleans it of ash before setting up the lamps.

sources.quote: שֶׁהִיא זָהָב טָהוֹר; דָּ"אַ עַל טָהֳרָהּ שֶׁל מְנוֹרָה, שֶׁמְּטַהֲרָהּ וּמְדַשְּׁנָהּ תְּחִלָּה מִן הָאֵפֶר
sources.says: Rashi says it is pure gold, or else it refers to the menorah's cleaning: he first clears it of ash.

24:7.headline: The incense is a 'reminder' that brings the bread before God
24:7.body: None of the bread on the table was burned for God. Rashi says only the frankincense was burned, and it serves as a reminder through which the bread is remembered above; Rabbeinu Bahya adds that through it blessing flows to the world's food.

sources.quote: שֶׁאֵין מִן הַלֶּחֶם לְגָבוֹהַּ כְּלוּם, אֶלָּא הַלְּבוֹנָה נִקְטֶרֶת
sources.says: Rashi says none of the bread goes to God; only the frankincense is burned.

sources.quote: וְהִיא לְזִכָּרוֹן לַלֶּחֶם, שֶׁעַל יָדָהּ הוּא נִזְכָּר לְמַעְלָה
sources.says: Rashi says the frankincense is a remembrance for the bread, through which the bread is remembered above.

sources.quote: כי מתוך שמקטירים הלבונה שעל הלחם הלחם נזכר למעלה והברכה תחול בו ממנו למזונות העולם
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says burning the frankincense makes the bread remembered above, and from it blessing comes to the world's food.

24:8.headline: Why 'on the Sabbath day' is said twice
24:8.body: The verse repeats 'on the Sabbath day'. Chizkuni says one is for setting out the new bread on the Sabbath and the other for burning the offering from the old bread on the Sabbath.

sources.quote: ביום השבת ביום השבת בשבת עורך חדשה ובשבת מקטיר ישנה
sources.says: Chizkuni says on the Sabbath he sets out the new bread, and on the Sabbath he burns the offering of the old.

24:11.headline: Did he pronounce God's name, or curse it?
24:11.body: The verb ויקב can mean to state outright or to curse. Onkelos and Rashi read it as pronouncing the special Name; Ibn Ezra notes others read it as cursing, as in Balaam's 'how can I curse', and prefers the first.

sources.quote: כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ "וּפָרֵשׁ", שֶׁנָּקַב שֵׁם הַמְיֻחָד וְגִדֵּף
sources.says: Rashi follows Onkelos: he spelled out the special Name and blasphemed.

sources.quote: יש אומרים שפירושו ויפרש כמו אשר פי ה׳‎ יקבנו אשר נקבו בשמות ויש אומרים שהוא כמו מה אקוב והראשון קרוב לפי דעתי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some read it as stating clearly, others as cursing like 'how can I curse', and he thinks the first is closer.

24:11.headline: Shelomit greeted everyone with 'shalom', and talked with everyone
24:11.body: Rashi reads both names of the blasphemer's mother. שלמית because she chattered 'peace to you' to all, and בת דברי because she spoke with every man, which led her astray.

sources.quote: דַּהֲוָה פִּטְפְּטָה "שְׁלָם עֲלָךְ", "שְׁלָם עֲלֵיכוֹן", מְפַטְפֶּטֶת בִּדְבָרִים
sources.says: Rashi says she would chatter 'peace to you, peace to you all', prattling away.

sources.quote: דַּבְּרָנִית הָיְתָה, מְדַבֶּרֶת עִם כָּל אָדָם, לְפִיכָךְ קִלְקְלָה
sources.says: Rashi says בת דברי means she was a talker who spoke with everyone, and so she went wrong.
